So our glorious Putt has already brought long-desired changes to Voat since officially becoming Voat CEO. Not to attribute all the praise to him; many of the comments Putt has made today referred to "we", as in he, Atko, and others like Cynabuns, FuzzyWords, and potentially others will all be working together to think, implement, and test changes to come.

First, the changes: Primarily what has been introduced is an expansion of the effect of the block user feature, which instead of just preventing abusive inbox pings now also auto-collapses comments from blocked users. There have also been significant additions to the reporting functionality on Voat.

The reception: from what I have seen virtually everyone supports the changes made today, and I myself am in this camp. I see nothing wrong with what has been implemented and perceive it as only offering more freedom to the users, not less, which is just about all I personally need to be satisfied. Still, I have seen a small number of complaints from a, well, vocal minority, and I figured I'd just discuss these criticisms.

There have been criticisms that expanding the block user feature in such a way is a slippery slope, that it fabricates a safe space on Voat. I understand the source of these concerns, but I feel like they are best addressed when emphasizing the difference between censorship and ignorance. As people often say, freedom of speech is not a right to an audience. It's true. People should be free to speak their mind, to say whatever they like, to doubt and question accepted norms. This does not mean that any individual should be obligated to listen to every person, regardless of their tone, vulgarity, or message. If you want to have an intellectual discussion then it would suit you well to listen to all viewpoints, but if some of the viewpoints being presented are either lacking substance or so weighed down with fallacy or gibberish that they become a burden, no one is expected to listen.

What the blocking feature does is make it easier for users who wish to ignore specific users to do so. The comments are collapsed. That's all. Voat is not removing any content posted by anyone who finds themselves blocked. This is not censorship of any form, and I see no compelling argument that this is a slippery slope to anything like censorship.

I also fail to see how this creates safe spaces, as the ideas or voices that certain people might not like to hear are not being removed, only ignored. If people choose to block users with substantial arguments that simply don't align with their own views, then the users choosing to block other users are closing their eyes to honest discussion, but that is a choice of theirs and in no way alters the actual state of the space or community that is Voat. The content remains, regardless of the source.

This leads me to my final point. Today Putt also said that soon a feature will be introduced that will allow moderators to remove content entirely, even killing links. This is mainly for content such as illegal content like CP, and in that sense I appreciate its necessity. As this feature is not yet implemented we should wait until actual details come forward before actually criticizing it, but I understand that some people might have concerns about how this feature could be used. Personally I am more of a fan of moving content rather than removing it, at least where subverse rules are considered, so as to avoid any criticisms about censorship (the insurance of /v/removed). That said I understand that with CP the content should be removed from Voat entirely. It is illegal, an incredibly small number of people actually want to see it, and the issues its presence here presents are far larger than whatever value might me meekly argued that it adds. As long as this feature is only utilized to deal with illegal content, I see no issues with it, either.

All and all I would say Voat is staying true to its path of freedom. Stay vigilant, goats.
